why: Removing house x only affects its own segment, and the change depends on whether x - 1 and x + 1 still exist: both present splits one segment into two (+1), neither present deletes a single-house segment (-1), one present just shrinks it (0). A hash set of living houses gives O(1) per query; the week's union-find is the reverse-time alternative.
hints: When one house disappears, can segments other than its own change?
Look only at the neighbours x - 1 and x + 1 after removal: two neighbours means a split (+1), zero means the segment vanishes (-1), one means no change.
Count initial segments as houses h with h - 1 absent, then process queries with a set. O(n + q).
pitfalls: Compute the initial count correctly: one segment per house whose left neighbour is missing.
Remove x from the set before (or independently of) checking its neighbours.
Positions may be negative or large; use a set, not an array.
statement:
Houses stand at distinct integer positions given in houses. They are destroyed one at a time in the order given by queries (every query is a house that exists, and no house is destroyed twice).

A segment is a maximal group of houses at consecutive integer positions. After each destruction, record how many segments remain. Return those counts in order.

Example: houses = [1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 9], queries = [6, 3, 7, 2, 9, 1]. Initially the segments are [1,2,3], [6,7], [9].

  • Destroy 6: [1,2,3], [7], [9] -> 3.
  • Destroy 3: [1,2], [7], [9] -> 3.
  • Destroy 7: [1,2], [9] -> 2.
  • Destroy 2: [1], [9] -> 2.
  • Destroy 9: [1] -> 1.
  • Destroy 1: nothing left -> 0.

Answer: [3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 0].
constraints:
• Numeric bounds are not stated in the source. Assume 1 <= houses.length <= 10^5, 1 <= queries.length <= houses.length and -10^9 <= houses[i] <= 10^9.
  • All values in houses are distinct; every query is in houses, and queries are distinct.
